“There is a huge amount of value in learning from people who have spent years working in the industry,” she says. “They can bring real situations, lessons learnt, and practical experience into a training environment in a way that is very difficult to replicate from theory alone.”
However, she notes that the outcomes differ. “An accredited programme leads to a formally recognised educational outcome and, depending on the programme, can also become a building block towards further learning. An experience-based course may offer excellent practical development, but it doesn’t automatically provide that same formal recognition.”
At the same time, Harris cautions against assuming learning has value only when it carries credits. A short session could help an agent improve negotiation skills, manage a difficult client conversation, or understand a particular aspect of a transaction.
“If someone has genuine expertise in a very specific area and can share knowledge that helps a property practitioner do their job better the next day, that is worthwhile learning,” she says. “Not everything needs to become a qualification.”
She says the problem arises when learners cannot distinguish between a specialist course, an accredited qualification, and recognised CPD. “There is absolutely room for all three, but the learner shouldn’t have to work out the difference afterwards.”
Independent training draws on a practitioner’s experience to address specific skills gaps and changing market demands. It can range from a short masterclass to a multi-day programme, focusing on practical application rather than a formal qualification.
Janine Barry, founder of Mega Agent Sales Mastery and owner of Janine Barry Property Group, was one of the founding broker-owners of RE/MAX of Southern Africa. She says she started her training business after identifying gaps in agents’ practical skills, and her programmes range from one-hour introductions to four-day courses. Since launching her masterclasses in June 2025, she says she has trained more than 2,600 agents.
“I was fascinated by the lack of skill sets and, let’s call it, passion, because knowledge creates passion in our business,” she says. “When you have the skills, and you have the knowledge, you do better.”
Barry believes agents must adapt to the many changes affecting the property market, particularly as property companies need to devote considerable time to legislation, contracts, compliance, and internal systems. She says this leaves less time to develop sales and interpersonal skills.
“I don’t train agents how to be an estate agent,” she says. “I train and educate agents to acquire the skill sets that help them serve their clients better on a higher level.”
Her courses offer certificates of attendance or completion, depending on the programme, but do not provide CPD points. She sees them as complementary to mandatory professional development. “There’s no conflict at all,” Barry says.
She follows up with participants after longer courses to assess how they apply what they have learnt, as she believes professional development doesn’t stop once an agent gains experience. “You can never, ever know it all, and you can never know enough,” says Barry.
In-house training focuses on the systems, operating standards, brand expectations, and practical processes agents need to work effectively within a particular business. For franchise groups, it also helps establish consistency across offices while allowing practitioners to apply their local market knowledge.
Gerhard Kotzé, chief executive officer of RealNet Holdings, says the balance between internal training and external expertise depends on the business model and practitioners’ experience.
“A property group needs internal training capacity to take ownership of its brand knowledge, operating standards, and the support its people receive,” he says. “External providers bring valuable expertise, but the group remains responsible for helping its people apply that knowledge within its own business.”
Kotzé also notes that internal programmes must evolve as technology, systems, and industry practices change.
“There will always be a place for internal brand training,” he says. “My preference is for this knowledge to be shared by well-rounded franchise managers who have been successful property practitioners themselves and, ideally, have also run estate agencies.”
Training must also connect brand standards with daily operations, supported by accessible systems and resources. “The objective is a consistent, professional experience for the consumer while allowing our franchisees to bring their local knowledge and entrepreneurial strengths to their businesses,” Kotzé says.
He sees formal education, CPD, specialist courses, and brand-specific training as complementary, with the appropriate mix changing throughout a practitioner’s career.
“A group that recruits large numbers of new entrants needs to invest substantially in structured internal training and ongoing guidance,” he says. He adds that experienced practitioners often need more specialised input to refine their skills and respond to changing market conditions.
Barry Fourie, national operations manager at Chas Everitt, shares Kotzé’s view that in-house training complements accredited providers. He says the Chas Academy provides practical skills training alongside the group’s systems and standards, while accredited providers deliver formal qualifications.
“The two forms of learning reinforce each other,” Fourie says. “An agent may understand a principle in a classroom but gain much more confidence when an experienced practitioner shows how to apply it in a real conversation or transaction.”
Fourie says mentorship matters most for newcomers, who need support applying what they learn in real-world situations. “The greatest opportunity lies in consistent coaching and mentorship,” he says. “Training can teach an agent what to do, but a new agent also needs guidance while learning how to do it well.”
He encourages new entrants to look beyond online courses for regular, face-to-face guidance from an experienced practitioner, sales manager, or principal. He supports independent specialist training, provided the trainer is reputable and the content relevant.
“If an agent comes away better equipped to serve clients and conduct business professionally, that is valuable development,” Fourie says.
Accredited education, independent specialist programmes, and in-house training each serve a purpose. The right combination depends on an agent’s experience, career objectives, and learning needs.
As Harris emphasises, it should be clear whether a course supports ongoing development or provides a recognised qualification or CPD points before anyone enrols. Non-accredited training can deliver genuine value, but its credibility depends on the trainer’s expertise, the relevance of the content, and transparency about what participants will receive.

headline: From home loans to listings: Private Property’s new CEO on agents, finance, and competition
body:
MAIN IMAGE: Wiehahn Koch – Private Property CEO
Private Property
Wiehahn Koch joined Private Property as chief executive officer in September, bringing a banking background. He says his first year will focus on understanding the business and sharpening what the portal offers agents, consumers, and partners.
Koch joins the portal from Capitec, where he most recently led embedded financial services, growing distribution through partner platforms. Before that, he helped launch and grow the bank’s home loans business.
Asked why he made the move, Koch said his financial services work had shown him the role a portal plays in buying a home. “What became increasingly clear to me is just how important the property platform is in the overall homeownership journey,” he said. He added that he sees scope for Private Property to do more “for consumers, for agents and for our partners”.
Koch said he intends to apply lessons from financial services. Chief among them is that platforms work best when they make it easier for different participants to create value together. “Private Property isn’t simply a website with listings. It’s an ecosystem connecting consumers, agents, developers, financial partners and other players in the property journey,” he said.
He said he wants to ask where friction exists in that journey, where technology can simplify things, and where partnerships can add value.
He took a similar view on finance. “Listings are an important starting point, but they’re not the destination,” he said. In his view, buyers also face questions about affordability, finance, insurance, legal processes, and moving. He added that the portal doesn’t necessarily provide all of these itself, but connects people with the right information, tools, and partners at the right time.
Koch said he does not plan to arrive with a fixed agenda. “I don’t want to come in assuming I know all the answers,” he said. He wants to start by understanding the business through its staff, agents, consumers, and partners.
From there, he wants to define a clearer value proposition for each group instead of treating them as a single customer base. For agents, he said, that means quality opportunities, better leads, and products that help them grow their businesses. For consumers, it means a more trusted property journey with less friction.
Estate agents are the portal’s core paying customers. Koch said they value its reach and brand but want clearer evidence of a return. “Agents tell us that they value the reach and brand of Private Property, but they also want to see a clear connection between what they’re investing in and the value they’re getting back,” he said. He described that expectation as reasonable.
On balancing large national agencies against independents and single-agent operators, he acknowledged that their needs differ. In his view, larger groups may need scale, data, and integration, while independents may need affordability, visibility, and tools to compete. “Our job is not to favour one model over another,” he said.
Koch said he plans to spend significant time with agents. He wants to learn what takes up their time, where leads fall out of the process, and what information they lack. “I don’t want to build a strategy for agents without building it with them,” he said.
Koch was asked whether the Competition Commission’s push towards a more open, interoperable portal market is a constraint or an opportunity. He said the portal should aim to be chosen for the value it delivers, “not because of friction or barriers elsewhere in the ecosystem”. He added that the regulatory environment reinforces the importance of transparency and fairness. If the portal gets that right, he said, openness becomes an opportunity rather than a threat.
Koch said technology and AI should remove friction across the property journey for both consumers and agents. For first-time buyers, he wants the portal to work as a connected whole rather than a series of separate touchpoints. That would cover everything from affordability and property search through to contacting an agent. “The technology should feel almost invisible, and the experience should just be easier,” he said.
Koch often quotes the line “If not us, who? If not now, when?”. Asked what that means for Private Property, he pointed to changes in consumer expectations, technology, and how people find, finance, and transact in property. He said the aim is to act now, not in reaction to competitors but to “shape what comes next”. “If we have the opportunity to improve the property journey for millions of South Africans, why wouldn’t we do it now?” he said.
Asked what he looks for in a listing, Koch said location comes first. He added that, as a golfer, he would also check whether there is a course nearby.

headline: Celebrating a fourth Corporate Vision award and the journey behind it
body:
MAIN IMAGE: Johann van der Merwe – CEO of WeconnectU
Advertorial
This month, Corporate Vision named WeconnectU Best Property Management Software Company – South Africa for the fourth year in a row.
The Technology Innovator Awards are a global programme recognising organisations that demonstrate excellence, innovation and forward-thinking approaches across the technology sector. The awards look beyond technology itself to recognise businesses delivering innovative solutions, creating measurable impact and setting new benchmarks within the markets they serve.
We’re incredibly proud of this achievement. Four consecutive wins is something worth celebrating. But we’re also very aware that none of them would have been possible without the property professionals who have been part of the WeconnectU journey.
The truth is, the WeconnectU receiving this award today is very different to the one that received it for the first time in 2023. Our solutions have grown, our ecosystem has become more connected and intelligent, and the challenges we are working with our clients to solve have become considerably more ambitious.
That progress hasn’t happened in isolation. It’s grown out of a close, two-way relationship with our clients and the wider property management industry, an industry that has itself changed enormously over the past decade. New pressures, expectations and opportunities have given us fresh problems to solve; the solutions we build have, in turn, helped property professionals find better ways to work and create value.
That constant exchange has kept us evolving alongside the industry we serve. It’s a huge part of how we’ve stayed at the forefront of property management technology and why this fourth consecutive award is something we could never celebrate alone.
The timing makes this year’s recognition even more meaningful. In 2027, WeconnectU turns ten.
From the beginning, our founders’ ambition was to use technology to help property professionals create more value from the role they already occupied. They knew first-hand how close property managers sit to the finances, operations, risks, maintenance needs and relationships that shape the assets in their care. The opportunity was to give them more capacity to apply that knowledge with greater insight and impact.
That thinking became the foundation of our purpose: creating more valued and valuable property managers.
Almost ten years later, that opportunity feels bigger than ever, especially with AI reshaping what technology can do.
AI can process and connect information at a scale and speed that would have been difficult to imagine when WeconnectU started. It can reduce repetitive work, identify patterns and help bring the right information into view sooner. We’re already integrating those capabilities into the WeconnectU ecosystem.
For property professionals, that creates even more room to focus on the work where experience, judgement and relationships matter most: understanding context, advising clients, making better decisions and managing assets more intelligently.
It also highlights another opportunity where WeconnectU is uniquely positioned to contribute as a technology partner.
Over the past decade, the WeconnectU ecosystem has expanded across Community Asset Management, Rental Asset Management and, through RedRabbit, inspections and maintenance management.
Today, more than 1.1 million professionally managed assets are connected through that ecosystem, generating an extraordinary volume of financial, operational, compliance, maintenance and property information.
The value of that scale lies in what we can learn from it and what we can give back to the industry.
In 2027, WeconnectU plans to release the inaugural South African Asset Intelligence Report, using aggregated, anonymised data from across our ecosystem to build a broader picture of professionally managed property assets across five dimensions: financial health, operational health, governance health, physical asset health and stakeholder experience.
The aim is to give property professionals richer context around the assets they manage: helping them identify trends and risks, benchmark performance and have more valuable conversations with their clients.
For us, it’s a natural progression.
Better technology has already transformed how much information property professionals can access. Now we have an opportunity to help turn that information into intelligence they can use.
That is the kind of progress we want the next decade to be about.
Technology will keep changing. AI will become more capable, data will become more useful, and many of the tasks that consume time today will become easier to automate or support.
That doesn’t make property professionals less valuable. It empowers them to be more so.
We want professionals across the industry to have more time and better information to advise, influence decisions, manage risk and take a more strategic role in the performance of the assets entrusted to them. In other words, to become even more valuable to their clients and more valued for the contribution they make.
That has been our purpose from the beginning, and it remains the direction we want to keep moving in.
Four consecutive Corporate Vision awards give us plenty to celebrate as we head towards ten years of WeconnectU. More than anything, though, they give us an opportunity to say thank you to the clients and property professionals who have trusted us, challenged us and shared this journey with us.
We’re incredibly proud of how far we’ve come together – and even more excited about where we’ll go next.

headline: Buyers hold their ground as banks raise the bar on deposits
body:
BetterBond
South Africa’s residential property market is holding steady despite renewed affordability pressure, according to BetterBond’s October 2026 Property Brief. Home loan activity recovered in the third quarter, house prices continued to grow faster than inflation and approval ratios improved in most regions. However, the brief notes that higher deposit requirements and the September increase in the prime lending rate are making it harder for some buyers to enter the market.
The BetterBond Index of Home Loan Applications rose by 2.4% quarter-on-quarter in Q3, recovering some of the ground lost in Q2 after the Reserve Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee began reversing the rate-cutting cycle in May. According to the brief, the average monthly number of applications over the first three quarters of 2026 is virtually on par with 2025.
House prices are still moving upwards. The average price for all buyers reached R1.7 million in Q3, up 1.8% year-on-year, while first-time buyers (FTBs) recorded 8.4% year-on-year growth. The brief points out that average house price growth now exceeds inflation, which stood at 4.4%, by a healthy margin. Buyers aged 51 to 60 recorded the strongest gains, with an average purchase price of R2.2 million over the 12 months to September and real growth of 11.4%. Buyers aged 31 to 40 also saw double-digit nominal price growth.
Deposits are the pressure point agents will need to watch. The brief describes lenders as uncertain about interest rate direction over the past year, with banks lowering deposit requirements seven times and raising them five times since September 2025. When the prime rate rose from 10.5% to 10.75% in September, banks reacted quickly, and Q3 ended with the average deposit requirement for all buyers 21.7% higher than a year earlier. FTBs fared better, with their average deposit up 5.6% year-on-year.
Rising incomes are helping to absorb some of that pressure. BetterBond recorded a new average homebuyer income of R74,000 a month in Q3. Over the past five years, homebuyer incomes have grown by an average of 4.7% a year in real terms, compared with 1.2% for GDP, and FTB incomes rose by 13.4% year-on-year. According to the brief, these income gains and the sound financial position of the major banks help explain the improvement in loan approval ratios.
In the 12 months to September 2026, North West was the only region where the ratio of loans granted to applications declined. Greater Pretoria remained the region with the highest approval ratio at 75%, followed by the Western Cape and KwaZulu-Natal at 72%. KwaZulu-Natal recorded the largest year-on-year improvement at 8.7%, followed by the Free State and Northern Cape at 6.8%.
On the supply side, the value of residential building plans passed rose by 8.4% year-on-year in the first seven months of 2026, with plans for flats and townhouses up 21%. Completions are lagging, however, with the completion ratio down 12% year-on-year over the same period, and the brief expects this slow pace to keep putting upward pressure on house prices. The Western Cape led the country with R6.2 billion worth of houses and flats completed between January and July, followed by Gauteng at R6 billion. Together with KwaZulu-Natal, these provinces accounted for 88% of the R16.2 billion total.
The construction sector itself is recovering. The Afrimat Construction Index rose by 5% quarter-on-quarter in real terms in Q2, and construction employment increased by 95,000 over the 12 months to June 2026. Dr Roelof Botha, economic advisor to BetterBond, says that because completed residential building values still trail house price growth, he expects a shortfall in this market down the line.
Interest rates remain the key uncertainty. Botha argues that because the recent rise in the Consumer Price Index is driven by supply-side factors and the labour market is static, tighter monetary policy may do more harm than good. He expects a normalisation of global fuel cargo shipments to bring inflation down sharply, which could pave the way for lower interest rates.
“There are encouraging signs of stability across the residential property market, with home loan activity holding up and house price growth continuing to outpace inflation,” says Stephan Potgieter, CEO of BetterHome Group Mortgage Origination and BetterBond. “At the same time, higher deposit requirements and renewed interest rate pressure mean affordability remains an important consideration for buyers.”
Read the full October 2026 BetterBond Property Brief here.

headline: South Africa’s housing market responds to shifting demand
body:
Advertorial
South Africa’s housing market is staying the course, with several indicators pointing to some improvement in affordability. While buyers still face higher deposit requirements and the possibility of renewed inflationary and interest rate pressures, home loan application data suggests the market is absorbing these challenges and sustaining activity, says BetterBond’s National Head of Sales, Bradd Bendall.
BetterBond’s latest (September) Property Brief shows that the Index of Home Loan Applications remained virtually unchanged during the first two months of the third quarter, following a marginal decline in the second quarter. “Notwithstanding May’s increase in the prime lending rate and the banks’ decision to increase their deposit requirements, home loan application volumes were still 11.3% higher in the third quarter than they were at the end of 2023,” says Bendall. “This means that buyers are still actively looking to engage in the property market by applying for bonds to finance their homes.”
Recent data provides a mixed view of buyer affordability. While the average price paid by first-time buyers has increased by 8% year-on-year, house-price-to-income ratios and deposit requirements have also improved. According to BetterBond’s latest Property Brief, the average first-time buyer house price now stands at R1.4 million; a nominal increase of 19% since the third quarter of 2023.
Across all buyers, average house prices have increased by 2.5% in real terms over the past three years. Nationally, prices rose by 5.9% over the past year, compared with 1.2% during the preceding 12-month period. Bendall adds that in addition to lower interest rates, the slow pace of new-home completions and growing supply deficit is helping to support this house-price growth.
However, longer-term income comparisons show improvements in affordability. For buyers aged between 41 and 50, the house-price-to-income ratio has fallen by 27% since 2021. This group now requires the equivalent of seven quarters of income to buy a home at the national average price, explains Dr Roelof Botha, Economic Advisor to BetterBond Home Loans.
Most age groups, apart from buyers aged between 21 and 30, also have lower house-price-to-income ratios than they did a decade ago, Botha adds. This suggests that homes may be relatively more affordable compared with incomes over the longer term, even though prices have risen in several segments of the market.
Deposits remain more manageable than they were two years ago. Despite the slight increase in July and August, the overall deposit requirement remains 7.3% lower than it was in 2024. “Unless interest rates rise again, it’s likely that deposit requirements will remain relatively stable for the rest of the year,” notes Botha.
Housing demand is also showing signs of broadening beyond the higher-income segment of the market. Since interest rates started to come down, the pattern of house price growth across different income groups has shifted, says Bendall. Buyers earning less than R15 000 a month continue to record the strongest growth, with average house prices in this group increasing by 8.8% over the past year.
There has also been a notable increase among buyers earning between R15 000 and R25 000 a month. Average house prices for this group rose by 6.5% over the past year, making it the second-fastest growing income group, up from fifth place previously. Meanwhile, the highest income group, earning more than R55 000 a month, moved from second to third place. “Importantly, house prices for these three income groups have increased faster than inflation,” says Botha. Consumer price inflation was 4.3% in July.
While this may benefit existing homeowners, it could pose some affordability challenges for first-time buyers entering the market, says Bendall. “For these buyers in particular, working with a bond originator who can approach multiple banks may help them secure a more favourable lending rate and improve their chances of qualifying for a home loan.”
Regional trends are playing an increasingly important role in the housing market. The Western Cape and Greater Pretoria have widened the gap over much of the rest of the country, recording double-digit house-price growth over the past year. Average house prices in the Western Cape increased by 13.8%, while Greater Pretoria recorded growth of 11.5%.
Bendall attributes some of the demand in these regions to their strong education offering, from quality schools and extra-mural activities to tertiary education opportunities. Pretoria also benefits from its role as South Africa’s administrative capital, with government departments, foreign embassies and other institutions supporting demand. Mpumalanga has overtaken KwaZulu-Natal to take third place in terms of average house prices, with homes selling for an average of R1.67 million.
Employment trends are also impacting regional housing demand. Over the 12 months to June 2026, the Western Cape, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal recorded meaningful employment gains. The Western Cape was the standout performer, adding 91 000 jobs – almost the same number as the jobs lost in Gauteng over the period. Gauteng nevertheless remains South Africa’s largest employment hub, accounting for 30% of total national employment.
BetterBond’s latest data suggests that the property market remains on relatively firm footing, despite continued pressure on households. Home loan applications remain above 2023 levels, deposits are lower than they were two years ago, the relationship between house prices and incomes has improved for most age groups, and the home loan approval ratio has risen to 64.5%. “A strong rand and easing inflation pressures could give the Reserve Bank room to maintain or eventually relax monetary policy in the next few months, although this outlook remains dependent on interest rates, oil prices and broader global conditions,” says Bendall.

headline: Retirees aren’t rightsizing: they’re risk-sizing
body:
MAIN IMAGE: Linda Piek, sales executive at RealNet RainMaker; Tiffiny Hancock, property practitioner at Harcourts Ambers
Kerry Dimmer
For years, the retirement property conversation has centred on downsizing. Then came rightsizing. Now there is risk-sizing.
Rightsizing asks, “What is the right home for the buyer?” Risk-sizing asks, “What could make this home the wrong one for the buyer later?” It raises the question property practitioners should be asking: what risks is the buyer actually trying to remove?
In investment and financial-risk contexts, risk-sizing is about determining the appropriate exposure to risk rather than simply focusing on the size of the investment. Applied to retirement property, the question becomes: how should a retiree choose a home that reduces the chance of another disruptive move later?
For the property practitioner, this changes the brief. It means looking beyond what suits the 65-year-old standing in front of you and considering whether the property could still work at 75, 80, or 85.
Linda Piek, sales executive at RealNet’s RainMaker business platform, who specialises in marketing retirement villages in Pretoria East, says retirees are increasingly buying less risk rather than simply less space.
“Yes, space is part of the equation, but risk reduction is often the real motivation.” She identifies financial, lifestyle, physical, and security risks, including rising municipal costs, maintenance, isolation, distance from healthcare and support networks, stairs, large gardens, and homes that become difficult to secure.
Agents no doubt already weigh these factors when matching retirees to properties, but are they really considering the buyer’s future? And is the buyer?
A useful test is to ask: if the buyer were 85 rather than 65, what would you tell them to look for? The point is not to assume that a healthy 65-year-old will suddenly become frail. It is to avoid selling them a property that only works while they remain exactly as they are today.
Buyers themselves appear to be thinking along these lines. According to Piek, one of the biggest shifts she is seeing is that retirees are no longer asking “How much house can I afford?” but rather “What kind of home gives me the greatest freedom?”
“For many buyers, the ideal retirement property is not the largest or the cheapest. It’s the one that reduces financial pressure, enhances security, supports independence, and remains suitable for the next 15 to 20 years of life.”
One risk that is easily overlooked is that the property is being bought by two people whose futures may not follow the same path. One partner may remain highly active while the other becomes less mobile, and Piek says failing to plan for this is a major oversight.
“Many buyers choose a home that suits them today rather than one that will suit them in 10 or 15 years. They overlook single-level living, wide doorways, step-free entrances, accessible bathrooms, and proximity to healthcare services.”
Tiffiny Hancock, a property practitioner at Harcourts Ambers, which specialises in retirement property across The Amber Developments in Howick, says buyers need to look further ahead. “I always ask whether this home will still work for them in 10 or 15 years. The last thing they want is to have to move again.”
That means considering whether there is sufficient space if one partner eventually requires assistance, whether bathrooms can accommodate changing mobility, and whether the remaining partner could continue living independently if the other could not. As Hancock puts it: “For me it is about finding a home that suits the way the retirees live now, but that can also work for them if their circumstances change.”
Agents should also be asking a question that has little to do with today’s purchase: who will buy this property in 10 or 15 years? A retirement property can represent a substantial share of a person’s accumulated capital, so future saleability is part of the risk assessment.
This includes the development’s age, competing developments, maintenance standards, levy history, accessibility, location, transport, healthcare provision, and the supply of similar units.
Sectional title, a popular choice for retirees who are not yet ready to move into a dedicated retirement village, introduces another long-term consideration. Buyers may be attracted by lower maintenance responsibilities, but the levy does not disappear when the home loan is paid off.
Piek and Hancock both note that buyers focused only on the purchase price often underestimate levies, rates and taxes, insurance, special levies, and care-related costs later in life. For an older owner living on retirement income, future levy increases are therefore not simply an inconvenience. They can become an affordability risk.
The agent should look beyond the levy amount to what it funds: the reserve fund, maintenance planning, insurance, communal facilities, staffing, infrastructure, and the history of special levies.
What happens between entry and exit? For retirement property, the questions agents can prompt retiree buyers to consider include:
These are not morbid questions. They are about making sure buyers understand the full property lifecycle.
Hancock says she has advised retirees against properties when she believed the home would not work for them in the longer term. “If I feel that the access is going to be difficult, the driveway might be too steep, the garden is going to become too much, or the layout simply isn’t going to work for that particular person in the long term, I will say so.
“I would much rather be honest with someone and help them find the right property than sell them something I don’t believe is going to work for them in the future.”
That, arguably, is the essence of risk-sizing.
“The most attractive retirement properties are often those that combine lifestyle benefits today with practical advantages for later life. This trend is commonly linked to the concept of ‘ageing in place’, where the goal is to remain independent in one suitable home for as long as possible,” says Piek.
Hancock advises buyers in this demographic not to wait until they “have” to move into a retirement estate. “Moving while they are still active gives them the opportunity to actually enjoy everything that retirement living offers. Then, if things do change as they age, they are already settled in their home, and they have the support and facilities available if needed.
“For me, that is really what good retirement living is about: enjoying independence now, but having peace of mind for the future.”

headline: MPC lifts repo rate to 7.25% as oil shock outweighs easing inflation
body:
Editor
The South African Reserve Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee has raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 7.25%, taking the prime lending rate to 10.75%. It is the second increase this year, following the May hike. Industry leaders agree that affordability will come under pressure, but they are divided on whether the decision was necessary. Most say the market is well placed to absorb it.
With one interest rate announcement left this year, Rhys Dyer, CEO of the ooba Group, says the increase is a reminder that, despite improving domestic inflation, global inflationary risks continue to weigh heavily on the interest rate outlook.
“While any increase in borrowing costs is disappointing for consumers and the property market at large, it is important to view today’s decision in context,” says Dyer. “Barring the 25-basis point interest rate hike in May this year, the previous increase was in May 2023, reflecting what has otherwise been a relatively stable and supportive bank lending environment.”
Dyer notes that annual consumer inflation edged up to 4.4% in August from 4.3% in July, slightly below market expectations, while core inflation eased to 4.1%. “Inflation remains fairly well contained for now and continues to move broadly in the right direction, offering some relief for households even as global price risks persist,” he says. He adds that the latest BER survey showed inflation expectations easing in the third quarter, with household expectations falling sharply, which suggests that inflationary pressures are not becoming entrenched domestically.
Samuel Seeff, chairman of the Seeff Property Group, believes the Bank should have looked past what he regards as a short-term spike. “The current inflationary spike is driven by temporary factors such as oil prices rather than runaway domestic demand,” he says.
Seeff says that although the market has remained resilient, interest rates that are higher than necessary have meant no real growth over the past three years, with national transaction volumes still about 16% below pre-pandemic levels. He also points out that the increase takes prime to its highest level since May 2025.
Even so, Seeff maintains that lending conditions remain fundamentally favourable, and that well-positioned buyers can still find good value before the next upward price cycle.
Herschel Jawitz, CEO of Jawitz Properties, says consumers face “some short to medium term pain until rates flatten and start to fall again”, with first-time buyers the most exposed. He notes that the increase comes on top of higher petrol prices.
He does not expect the hike to derail the market. “Market activity remains firm, with demand from buyers outstripping supply, making house price growth more resilient even with the latest rate increase,” he says. According to the FNB Property Price Index, national house price growth moderated to 4.9% in August, which Jawitz says still sits marginally above inflation. He adds that the banks remain highly competitive on rate concessions.
Ryan Greeff, CEO of Quay 1, describes the hike as largely anticipated. He links it to the Middle East conflict, which has pushed oil above $100 a barrel and kept the rand under pressure, rather than to any meaningful deterioration in the domestic economy. He points out that prime remains well below the 11.75% highs of 2024.
In Cape Town, the timing coincides with one of the busiest periods in the property calendar, as spring and year-end deadlines such as school registrations and relocations bring buyers back into the market. “That seasonal motivation does not disappear simply because borrowing conditions have become slightly less favourable,” says Greeff.
His advice to buyers waiting on the sidelines is not to count on relief in the near term. “Two hikes in four months signal steadily increasing affordability pressure. The window to transact under still-workable conditions remains open, but it is narrowing.”

headline: How MortgageMarket’s new AI agent, Zero Capture, just solved the industry’s biggest problem: data capture
body:
MAIN IMAGE: Tim Akinnusi – CEO of MortgageMarket
Advertorial
For decades, the journey to South African homeownership has been bottlenecked by an industry norm: manual data entry. Consumer banking has catalysed the industry via mobile apps and instant clearing, however the mortgage origination pipeline historically relied consistently on heavy administration, a primary industry friction. A single home loan application routinely demanded around 45 minutes of tedious input and retyping across disparate lender systems, multiplying human error and effectively delaying bank approvals. 
Today marks the end of that administrative tax. Following the official launch at the Country Club Johannesburg on the 22nd September, MortgageMarket has officially launched ZeroCapture. South Africa’s first purpose-built, secure AI agent engineered specifically for mortgage origination. 
ZeroCapture was not an off the shelf acquisition. Its genesis began as an internal company-wide challenge: how could every team member actively integrate generative AI into their daily operational workflows? This experimentation yielded immediate productivity gains, and leadership quickly realized that general-purpose AI models wouldn’t solve the complex regulatory, credit, and underwriting realities of South African lending. 
The breakthrough came when MortgageMarket shifted from using generic AI tools to engineering its own specialised agent. 
ZeroCapture functions as an autonomous operational partner. It ingests complex buyer financial documentation in real time, with 100% completion rate. Originators and applicants review and verify their data before sign-off. It maps critical credit parameters directly into multi-bank submission formats. Where a human originator previously juggled multiple portal screens, ZeroCapture executes the entire distribution layer simultaneously. It is an autonomous origination agent engineered from the ground up to execute one job: originate a South African home loan faster and more accurately than legacy manual workflows ever permitted. 
For buyers and originators, the entire user experience collapses into a single streamlined motion. 
The applicant uploads their foundational document pack once: 
Within seconds, ZeroCapture extracts the data, verifies credentials against credit bureaus, and cross-checks employer and income consistency. Instead of an originator spending 45 minutes toggling between separate bank systems to manually re-enter identical fields, ZeroCapture sanitizes the data into each bank’s proprietary format and distributes the file simultaneously to all major lenders in real time. 
By compressing what was previously 45 minutes worth of admin into an under-five-minute digital flow, the platform delivers a verified 40-minute dividend on every submission. 
The commercial dividend compounds downstream. Because applications arrive clean, verified, and pre-structured to exact credit policies on first contact, lender queries plummet, rework cycles disappear, and first-time bank approval ratios lift substantially for buyers and partner brokers alike. 
In an era saturated with superficial artificial intelligence claims, MortgageMarket is deliberate about setting expectations. The company is adamant that technology alone is never the differentiator. 
“There has never been a more extraordinary time to build in business, but great technology is nothing without the people who understand the market,” says Tim Akinnusi, Chief Executive Officer of MortgageMarket. “ZeroCapture is not here to replace human expertise. Our competitive edge has always been our people and our fearless culture. This AI agent handles the structural friction so our mortgage specialists and partner brokers can deliver unprecedented client advisory.” 
This human-centric philosophy underpins MortgageMarket’s four pillars: People, Culture, Mission, and Technology. Algorithms process and package 
data at machine speed, but human intuition, empathetic counsel, and deep institutional relationships remain the driving force that gets home loans approved and support South Africans in achieving their home ownership goals. 
The live deployment of ZeroCapture today pioneers a structural shift across South Africa’s mortgage landscape. With upcoming platform expansions already slated to integrate bespoke bank partnerships and expanded insurance comparative models, MortgageMarket is systematically rewriting property finance infrastructure. 
For South African homebuyers, originator business owners and real estate partners, the era of endless paperwork and multi-portal fatigue ends today. ZeroCapture proves that when proprietary AI agents are built around real market friction, technology becomes an everyday commercial superpower. 
This is not an end point, but the first game point in a completely reimagined homeownership journey.

headline: Inflation gains on rental growth as Western Cape sets the pace
body:
PayProp
South Africa’s residential rental market recorded its strongest quarterly growth in more than a year in Q2 2026. However, the latest PayProp Rental Index reveals significant differences in performance across the country’s provincial rental markets, and rising inflation meant that real-terms returns were the weakest in almost two years.
Agencies will need to be vigilant about arrears to protect landlords’ shrinking margins.
Rental growth reached 5.2% year on year during the quarter, accelerating for a second consecutive quarter and taking the average national rent to a new high of R9 715, up R497 from a year ago.
Monthly rental growth also strengthened as the quarter progressed, rising from 4.7% in April to 5.3% in May and 5.6% in June – the fastest monthly growth recorded since February 2025.
“It’s encouraging to see rental growth accelerate for a second consecutive quarter, but Q2 also shows just how differently provincial rental markets are performing,” says Michelle Dickens, Commercial Director at PayProp.
The Western Cape set the pace in Q2, recording phenomenal rental growth of 9.7%, its highest since Q4 2024.

Average rent in the province reached R12 561, R1 107 more than a year ago and R436 higher than in Q1. Western Cape tenants now pay R1 999 more on average than tenants in the country’s second most expensive rental market, the Northern Cape.

The strength of the Western Cape market had a distorting impact on the national result. While national growth accelerated, seven of South Africa’s nine provinces recorded rental growth below the national average during Q2. PayProp calculates that if the Western Cape is removed, national rental growth falls to 4.3%, below CPI inflation.

Despite the rapid increase in rents, tenant payment performance in the Western Cape has remained strong. Just 12.3% of tenants in the province were in arrears in Q2, the lowest percentage ever recorded for any province in the PayProp Rental Index.

However, affordability should be no less of a focus in the province than in others. More than a quarter (27.5%) of Western Cape rental properties now cost more than R15 000 to rent, restricting a tenant with a budget of R7 500 to less than a quarter of the available rental stock in the province.
Elsewhere, the North West was the only other province to outperform national rental growth, accelerating from 6.5% in Q1 to 7.8% in Q2. Average rent reached R7 679 in the latest quarter, up R554 year on year.
Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal remained closely matched with rental growth of 4.4% and 4.2% respectively. Their average rents were even closer, at R9 646 in Gauteng and R9 657 in KwaZulu-Natal – a difference of just R11.

Some of Q1’s strongest performers lost momentum. Northern Cape rental growth slowed sharply from 12.9% in Q1 to 4.3% in Q2, while Limpopo recorded growth of 4.1%, its lowest rate since Q4 2021.
At the bottom end of the table, Mpumalanga remained South Africa’s slowest-growing rental market with annual rent inflation of just 2.3% in Q2, although this was an improvement from 0.4% in Q1. Free State rental growth also recovered to 3.3%.

“Provincial performance can shift significantly from one quarter to the next,” says Dickens. “For landlords and rental professionals, up-to-date local market data is essential when setting rents and assessing the performance of a rental property.”
Inflation closes the gap
While rental growth accelerated in Q2, inflation also increased throughout the quarter, reaching 5.0% in June.

Rental growth therefore remained ahead of inflation, but only narrowly. In real terms, growth is now at its weakest since Q3 2024, despite the improvement in nominal rental growth.

For landlords, the narrowing gap is important as it means the cost of owning and maintaining a rental property may also be going up. “Stronger rental growth is positive, but it needs to be viewed in the context of the wider cost environment,” says Dickens. “The margin over inflation has narrowed, and that will be important to watch over the remainder of the year.”
Arrears edge up from record low
Tenant payment performance remains strong nationally, although there was a small increase in the proportion of tenants in arrears.

In Q2, 16.9% of tenants were behind on their rent, up from the record low of 16.7% recorded in Q1. Despite the increase, this remains the joint-second lowest arrears level ever recorded in the PayProp Rental Index, but agents should be on the lookout for further rises in Q3 and Q4. Among tenants who were in arrears, the average amount owed improved slightly, from 74.3% of one month’s rent in Q1 to 73.5% in Q2.

There are signs that payment pressure could increase. PayProp notes that the May interest rate hike will push up tenants’ debt repayments, which account for around half of the average tenant’s income. Arrears typically lag interest rate changes by around six to nine months, meaning the impact could become visible around the new year.

For PayProp, Q2’s stronger rental growth is a positive result, but the combination of uneven provincial performance, rising inflation and potential pressure on tenant finances means the second half of the year will require close attention.

“Arrears remain close to record lows, which is encouraging,” says Dickens. “But the Q2 results show why landlords and rental professionals need to look beyond national averages. Rental growth, tenant affordability and payment performance can differ significantly from one market to another, and those local conditions are ultimately what determine achievable rents.”

headline: The five pillars of healthy property asset management
body:
MAIN IMAGE: Danie van der Merwe – director of solutions management at WeconnectU
Advertorial
What does it actually mean to manage a property asset well?
We talk about properties being “well managed” all the time, but if you ask ten property professionals what that actually means, you’ll likely get ten completely different answers.
Is a rental property well managed because the rent is collected every month? Is a community scheme well managed because its finances are in order? Because it’s compliant? Because maintenance happens on time? Because its trustees and owners are happy?
The fact is, all of those things matter, but none tells the whole story. If we’re serious about quantifying how well property assets are being managed – and we should be, if we’re going to demonstrate the industry’s true value – we need a more complete way to define what “well managed” actually looks like.
That’s the thinking behind the Property Asset Management Health Framework we are developing.
Rather than relying on any single indicator, the framework identifies five areas of property asset management that can be observed, measured and tracked over time. Each offers a different perspective on how well an asset is being managed. Together, they give us a far more reliable view of its overall management health.
Here’s what we’re talking about.
Financial health is about more than tracking whether money is coming in. It considers the quality and sustainability of that income, and the risks surrounding it.
For rental assets, that means analysing indicators such as rent, arrears, deposits and revenue per asset. For community assets, it includes levies, debt, collection activity and cost pressures affecting long-term financial sustainability.
Together, these indicators reveal whether the asset is on a sound financial footing – or where pressure may be starting to build.
Even the best asset management strategy means very little if the day-to-day work behind it isn’t being executed consistently.
Inspection activity, maintenance workflows, payments, debt actions, communications and recurring tasks all provide useful signals of whether the operation has the structure and capacity to deliver reliably.
Delays, bottlenecks and growing task loads can reveal pressure points long before they become obvious to clients.
Good governance and compliance create the guardrails for responsible property asset management, ensuring decisions are properly made and recorded, obligations are met, and stakeholders are protected.
In rental management, mandates, leases, FICA processes, deposit handling, inspection records, arrears processes and audit trails all contribute to the picture. In community management, key indicators include trustee decisions, approvals, meetings, financial controls, insurance, statutory obligations and audit readiness.
Together, these signals can expose gaps in accountability, documentation or process before they become legal, financial or reputational risks.
A property’s condition is one of the most visible expressions of how well it is being managed over time.
For rental assets, inspections, recommendations, maintenance activity, recurring defects and repair trends provide a growing record of that condition. For community assets, maintenance planning, infrastructure pressures, repairs, insurance and reserve planning broaden the picture.
Tracking these signals helps identify patterns early enough to plan, prioritise and prevent avoidable deterioration and cost.
Not every indicator of healthy asset management sits neatly on a balance sheet or maintenance schedule. Stakeholder experience matters too – and can be measured with reasonable confidence.
Communication, reporting, responsiveness, transparency and meeting discipline all indicate whether investors, trustees and owners have the visibility and confidence needed for good decision-making.
This is also where much of professional property management becomes visible to the client.
Strong stakeholder experience builds trust in the management process; poor visibility and communication can undermine that confidence even when much of the work behind the scenes is being done well.
The real power of the framework works in two directions.
Tracking effectiveness across the five pillars shows property professionals where strong outcomes are being achieved and where there is room to improve – creating opportunities to continually raise the quality of asset management services.
At the same time, connecting actions to outcomes makes professional value far more visible to clients. An inspection becomes evidence of proactive asset protection. Arrears management demonstrates income protection. Strong governance shows risk being actively managed.
The result is an opportunity to become both more valuable in the service delivered and more valued for the outcomes achieved.
The five pillars give property professionals a structured way to track management health within their own portfolios. But those measurements become far more meaningful when viewed within industry context.
This is where WeconnectU has an important contribution to make. With more than 1.4 million professionally managed assets connected across our rental and community management, inspections and maintenance solutions, we have a unique opportunity to responsibly aggregate anonymised operational data to begin building that broader context.
The Property Asset Intelligence Report we are currently developing is intended to become an important next step in this journey, bringing together signals across the five pillars to help property professionals benchmark their own results, identify emerging trends and better understand what healthy property asset management looks like across the industry.
For us, this is about more than publishing data. It’s about using our position as a software partner to help move the industry forward, giving property professionals the insight to keep raising the standard of the service they deliver, demonstrate their impact more confidently and ultimately become both more valuable and more valued.
There is still work to be done as we bring the framework, data and industry context together, but we believe the opportunity is significant.
As this initiative develops, we look forward to sharing more about how Property Asset Intelligence can help create a clearer, richer understanding of healthy property asset management in South Africa and further equip property professionals to deliver greater value to the clients and assets they serve.

headline: The invisible listing: why poor property data could cost sellers, buyers
body:
MAIN IMAGE: Fritz Swanepoel, CEO of Leapfrog Property Group
Fritz Swanepoel
Property search is starting to look a little different. For Fritz Swanepoel, CEO of Leapfrog Property Group, the shift is not just about another clever digital tool. As international property portals move towards conversational, AI-powered search, the information captured by agents could play a bigger role in whether a seller’s home is found — or quietly missed altogether.
“For years, we have written property listings primarily for people,” says Swanepoel. “Increasingly, we will also need to structure them for the technology helping people search. That does not make the human side of property marketing less important, but it does mean that attractive photographs and a beautifully written description may no longer be enough.”
Traditional property searches are built around filters. Buyers select an area, price range, number of bedrooms, number of bathrooms and perhaps a few additional features such as a swimming pool, garage or security estate.
That approach works when buyers know precisely what they want and when the available filters accurately reflect their priorities. But real people do not always think about homes in neat categories.
A buyer may instead be looking for a property that allows two people to work from home, accommodates large dogs, is close to good schools, has reliable backup power and will not require extensive maintenance. Another may want a home suitable for an elderly parent without necessarily searching for a formally designated multigenerational property.
Internationally, major property platforms are beginning to allow consumers to express these requirements in everyday language. Instead of selecting a series of boxes, buyers can increasingly describe the kind of life they want to live and ask technology to identify the properties that appear to match.
“This is an important shift because property has always been about far more than bedrooms and bathrooms,” says Swanepoel. “Buyers are not really searching for three bedrooms and two bathrooms. They are searching for a particular way of living. Technology is becoming better at understanding that distinction.”
That opens up real possibilities, but it also exposes a simple problem.
An AI-powered search can only work with the information available to it. If a property has excellent backup power but the listing merely says “solar”, the system may not know whether that means two panels for a geyser or a complete inverter and battery installation.
If the home has a separate room perfectly suited to working remotely, but it is described only as a “study”, it may not appear in a search for a dual work-from-home property. If pets are permitted in a sectional-title development but that information has not been captured, the home could be excluded from a pet-friendly search.
“The technology may be intelligent, but it cannot reliably discover information that was never recorded,” Swanepoel says. “That means poor listing data will no longer merely make an advertisement less informative. It could prevent the right buyer from seeing the property at all.”
The risk is particularly relevant in South Africa, where buyers increasingly consider features that are not always captured consistently across property listings.
These include the capacity and ownership status of solar and battery systems, boreholes and water-storage capacity, fibre availability, security infrastructure, sectional-title rules, accessibility, work-from-home suitability, municipal reliability, monthly levies and the true running costs of the property.
In a previous article, Swanepoel argued that governance has become part of location. Buyers increasingly want to understand whether municipal services are reliable, infrastructure is maintained and additional investment will be required to make a home resilient.
The industry now has to make sure that listing information reflects those day-to-day realities, not just the obvious features of the home.
“A home with dependable services, well-managed infrastructure and properly maintained communal facilities may offer a very different ownership experience from a similar looking home a few kilometres away,” he says.
“Technology may recognise a difference in price, but unless the underlying information is detailed and reliable, it may not understand why that difference exists. The property professional remains responsible for providing the context.”
This does not mean that agents should make unsupported claims about municipalities or attempt to predict future service delivery. It means they should understand and accurately communicate the practical factors that affect the property and the buyer’s likely experience of owning it.
Swanepoel cautions against interpreting the shift as the end of good property writing.
Buying a home remains an emotional decision. Buyers still need to imagine themselves living in the space, raising a family, entertaining friends or beginning a new chapter of their lives. Photographs, video and carefully considered language remain essential to creating that connection.
But the emotional story needs a stronger factual backbone than it may have needed in the past.
“The best property marketing will combine the two,” he says. “It will capture the feeling of the home while also providing accurate, structured information about how that home functions.”
A description that promises “effortless modern living” may create interest, but it tells a search system very little. A listing that accurately records energy resilience, security, connectivity, accessibility and operating costs gives both the technology and the buyer something meaningful to work with.
In practice, the strongest listings will need both: marketing that makes a buyer care, and data that helps the right buyer find the property in the first place.
There is also a temptation to respond by capturing as much information as possible. Swanepoel believes the priority should be accuracy rather than volume.
Incorrect information can cause more damage than missing information. An AI system can distribute and repeat an error faster than a human being, potentially presenting assumptions as established facts.
If a solar installation is financed or leased, that must be disclosed. If a room is marketed as a bedroom, it should legitimately function as one. If a development is described as pet-friendly, the applicable body corporate rules and approval requirements must be understood.
“The more technology relies on our information, the greater our responsibility to verify it,” says Swanepoel. “AI does not remove accountability from the property practitioner. It increases the importance of that accountability.”
Agents will need to ask better questions when taking mandates, inspect properties more carefully and distinguish between what has been verified, what the seller has represented and what still requires confirmation.
There is a tendency to assume that better property technology will gradually reduce the role of the property practitioner. Swanepoel believes the opposite may be true for practitioners who adapt.
Technology can search, compare and organise information, but someone must ensure that the information is correct. Someone must understand why one street performs differently from another, how a particular body corporate is managed and whether a property’s features genuinely meet the buyer’s needs.
“That is where local knowledge becomes even more valuable,” he says. “The agent’s role moves beyond simply uploading a property and waiting for an enquiry. The practitioner becomes the person who translates a real home, in a real community, into information that both people and technology can understand.”
The practitioners who succeed will not be those who attempt to compete with technology on speed. They will be those who provide the accuracy, judgment, context and accountability that technology cannot produce by itself.
The property industry has traditionally treated listing information as an administrative requirement and the description and photographs as the marketing.
That divide is becoming much harder to maintain.
Every verified feature, accurately captured cost and clearly explained restriction can influence whether a property is matched with a prospective buyer. The information sitting behind the advertisement is becoming part of the advertisement itself.
“For sellers, the message is straightforward,” Swanepoel concludes. “The quality of your mandate and the quality of the information captured about your home will matter increasingly. You are not only appointing someone to advertise the property. You are appointing someone to ensure that the market can properly understand it.”
“For property professionals, the challenge is just as clear. Tomorrow’s most effective listing will not simply be the one with the best wording. It will be the one that is accurate, complete, compelling — and visible to the buyer who is genuinely looking for that kind of home.”
In the next generation of property search, a home may be perfectly suited to a buyer and still never appear on their screen. The difference could come down to the quality of the data captured at the very first listing appointment.

headline: High Court declares B-BBEE certificate requirement for property practitioners unconstitutional
body:
MAIN IMAGE: Piet le Roux – CEO of Sakeliga, Thato Ramaili – CEO of the PPRA, Jan le Roux – CE of Rebosa
Editor
The Pretoria High Court has declared unconstitutional the requirement that property practitioners hold a B-BBEE certificate to be issued with a Fidelity Fund Certificate (FFC), the licence a business needs to trade lawfully.
The ruling follows a case brought by business organisation Sakeliga in 2024, after the Property Practitioners Regulatory Authority (PPRA) declined to issue FFCs to businesses that did not first provide a B-BBEE certificate. Operating without an FFC is a criminal offence.
The court has now struck down section 50(a)(x) of the Property Practitioners Act 22 of 2019, which the organisation identifies as the statutory foundation of the requirement.
Sakeliga describes the outcome as a major victory against using B-BBEE as a precondition for trading in the property sector, which it says generates upwards of R60 billion a year. According to the organisation, the ruling frees those defined in the legislation as property practitioners from compulsory participation in B-BBEE and saves resources that would otherwise go towards compliance and certification.
In Sakeliga’s view, the requirement was designed to compel participation rather than collect information. It points to the PPRA’s answering affidavit, which it says stated that the purpose of the limitation was to “ensure that those who pay lip service to transformation are not permitted to practice as property practitioners and earn an income from it”. It also cites the PPRA’s heads of argument, in which counsel reportedly submitted that “a purely voluntary transformation-reporting system would undermine the Act’s statutory design and the Authority’s ability to monitor and implement transformation measures”.
The organisation maintains that a B-BBEE certificate is a political instrument of the state rather than a business requirement, and that using licensing for what it calls race-restrictive purposes is an unacceptable barrier to the freedom to trade. It has repeatedly cautioned that government and regulators are seeking to make participation in B-BBEE and other race-based programmes, including employment equity targets, a precondition for economic activity across sectors.
The court also partly upheld Sakeliga’s challenge to the Act’s definition of “property practitioner”, finding certain elements irrational, overbroad, and unconstitutional. The narrowed definition, the organisation says, means several categories of people engaged in property-related business now fall outside the regulator’s reach. It adds that private owners, certain advertisers, and people dealing with specified property interests outside the ordinary course of business are no longer regarded as property practitioners. However, it did not secure the full narrowing it had sought and says it is assessing further legal options.
On the licence itself, Sakeliga states that the PPRA may no longer refuse an FFC because an applicant does not hold a B-BBEE certificate. Whether that applies immediately is disputed.
A declaration that part of an Act is unconstitutional does not become final on its own. Under the Constitution, the Constitutional Court must confirm it, and a court may grant interim relief to govern the position while it awaits confirmation. The PPRA and Rebosa read the order differently.
The PPRA’s position is that nothing changes yet. In response to Property Professional, chief executive Thato Ramaili said: “The orders of the High Court regarding the unconstitutionality of parts of section 1(b) of the definition of property practitioner, and the entirety of section 50(a)(x) of the PPA, are suspended; the unconstitutionality and interim order will take effect from the date on which the Constitutional Court confirms the declaration and effects the ruling.”
Ramaili added that, in practice, the requirement had not been a barrier to licensing. “As the PPRA, we have been issuing FFCs irrespective of the level of compliance. Since 2024 we have never refused to issue any practitioner with an FFC based on the level, and have accepted valid certificates and affidavits,” he said.
Rebosa disagrees, pointing to interim relief in the order. Jan le Roux, chief executive of Rebosa, said: “I disagree with the interpretation of the PPRA since the Judge in Point 8 of the order clearly states that, pending the decision of the Constitutional Court, the PPRA may not refuse to issue a Fidelity Fund Certificate on non-compliance with Section 50(a)(x) of the PP Act. The same applies to the ‘amended’ reading of the definition of Property.”
The judgment also addressed a recent question raised online: whether property websites that merely host listings must register as property practitioners. Le Roux said the order settles it. “This order also puts an end to the unnecessary polemic on social media about the so-called necessity of property portals to have to register as property practitioners. The judge said that a person whose involvement goes no further than ‘carrying, hosting, publishing or disseminating advertisements placed by another person and who does not otherwise participate in the sale, marketing, promotion or advertising of the property or property interest concerned’ is excluded from the definition of property practitioner.”
Le Roux added that the ruling does not remove the industry’s responsibility to transform. “This order does not negate the necessity to promote transformation in this industry actively, and Rebosa remains committed to playing a positive role in this regard,” he said. He also welcomes the fact that estate agents no longer have to bear the unnecessary expense of having to produce B-BBEE certificates in order to obtain their FFCs.
The PPRA was ordered to pay Sakeliga’s costs, including the costs of two counsel.
Because the judgment concerns the constitutionality of an Act of Parliament, the Constitutional Court will refer it for confirmation. Should the declaration be confirmed, Parliament will have 24 months to correct the definition.
Read the full judgment here

headline: Jobs, schools, and the capital effect: where property demand is strongest
body:
BetterBond
The Western Cape and Greater Pretoria are pulling further ahead of the rest of the country on house price growth, according to the September 2026 edition of the BetterBond Property Brief, which points to employment, schooling, and the pull of the administrative capital as the main forces reshaping where demand is strongest.
Over the past year, both regions recorded double-digit increases in average house prices. The brief places the Western Cape in pole position with growth of 13.8%, followed by Greater Pretoria at 11.5%. It attributes the stronger demand in these areas partly to the prevalence of schools offering quality education and extra-mural activities, especially sport, and to the presence of well-regarded tertiary institutions. Pretoria, the brief notes, carries the added advantage of being the country’s administrative capital, home to the Union Buildings, government ministries, and foreign embassies.
There has also been movement further down the table. The brief reports that Mpumalanga has leapfrogged KwaZulu-Natal into third place for average house prices, at R1.67 million.
Much of this, the brief argues, comes back to where the jobs are. It describes the availability of work as a key driver of regional migration, a trend it says continues to change the country’s demographics and, with it, the availability and prices of houses. Over the 12 months to the end of June 2026, the brief says three provinces attracted people from other parts of the country through meaningful gains in employment.
The Western Cape again stood out. The brief records a gain of 91 000 new jobs in the province, a figure it describes as virtually identical to the number of jobs lost in Gauteng over the same period. Mpumalanga recorded the second largest increase at 47 000 jobs, followed by KwaZulu-Natal with 23 000. The Eastern Cape and North West, by contrast, shed jobs over the past four quarters. Even so, the brief points out that Gauteng remains firmly in the top spot, accounting for 30% of the country’s total employment of roughly 16.7 million.
For practitioners, the pattern is a useful read on where competition for stock and buyer demand is likely to intensify. The regions drawing workers are, on the brief’s own account, the regions posting the strongest price growth, which suggests the divergence between provinces may persist rather than even out in the short term.
The regional picture sits within a national market the brief characterises as steadier than a year ago. It reports that the average house price across the country rose 5.9% year on year, compared with only 1.2% over the previous 12 months. First-time buyers are now paying an average of R1.4 million, which the brief describes as a nominal increase of 19% since the third quarter of 2023, while the home loan approval rate has climbed to 64.5%. The benchmark lending rate has held at 10.5% over the past three months.
Stephan Potgieter, chief executive officer of BetterHome Group Mortgage Origination and BetterBond, is quoted in the brief as saying: “There are some encouraging signals in the market, from improving home loan approval rates to stronger employment and continued growth in house prices. While buyers remain sensitive to interest rates and deposit requirements, affordability has improved for many South Africans. These trends point to a market where opportunities remain for those ready to take their next step towards homeownership.”
The brief’s economic commentary, provided by economist Dr Roelof Botha, adds that the recent decline in South Africa’s long-term bond yield suggests scope for further easing of monetary policy, with the consumer price index having dropped to marginally above the new upper tolerance level of 4%. It cautions, however, that any further rate relief will depend in part on external factors, including conditions in global energy markets.
For now, the brief’s regional data offers agents a clear signal on where the momentum lies, with the Western Cape, Pretoria, and Mpumalanga the areas to watch as buyers follow the jobs.

headline: Is a home loan prequalification necessary in today’s market?
body:
MAIN IMAGE: Rhys Dyer – CEO of ooba Group
ooba Home Loans
South Africa’s property market remains primed for investment. The cumulative impact of the previous six rate cuts since September 2024, together with competitive bank lending, continues to support buyer activity and encourage more first-time homebuyers to enter the market.
However, when it comes time to buy, some may question whether a Prequalification Certificate – also known as a Qualified Buyers Certificate – truly gives them the ‘edge’ in today’s housing market.
“Often underestimated, this document can offer significant benefits,” says Rhys Dyer, CEO of the ooba Group, adding that potential homebuyers can easily log on to free platforms like ooba’s Bond Indicator tool to check one’s credit score, understand their affordability and receive a pre-approval certificate all within a few minutes.
Dyer explains the difference between the prequalification and a pre-approval process – terms that are often used interchangeably by the market at large, adding that there is a clear difference.
“A pre-approval is a quick and simple way to determine what you can afford and what your credit score is by using an online pre-approval tool like the ooba Bond Indicator (OBI),” says Dyer. “It increases your chances of having offers accepted by sellers and helps you to make adjustments to your finances as needed.
He adds that accessing a service like the OBI should be step 1 in every homebuyer’s journey. “Available free online, the tool allows prospective buyers to check their credit score, determine their indicative affordability and receive a pre-approval certificate within minutes. This gives buyers an early indication of their home loan prospects and, importantly, a realistic price range in which to begin their property search.”
The next step is to obtain a Qualified Buyers Certificate (QBC) which takes the process a step further.
“A Qualified Buyers Certificate is a more robust version of a prequalification. It is conducted by a home finance expert who carefully evaluates your affordability in much the same way banks do. Documents are assessed, in-depth credit checks are performed, and your financial position is determined before you receive the certificate,” says Dyer.
He adds that a Qualified Buyers Certificate’s secret weapon lies in its ability to mimic the steps a bank takes when analysing a homebuyer’s finances after they’ve applied for a home loan.
“A Qualified Buyers Certificate places you – the homebuyer – in an elevated position as a ‘qualified buyer’, giving you more bargaining power when it comes time to negotiate the terms and conditions of the property sale agreement,” he says. “It is often conducted as a precursor to a home loan application and saves on approval times.”
Adding to its appeal is its high success rate, with ooba Home Loans’ data showing that 91.6% of its customers with a prequalification went on to have their home loans approved in August ‘26, compared to 91.2% average during H1 ’26 and 90.8% during H1 ’25.
“While a Qualified Buyers Certificate closely mirrors the affordability and credit assessments undertaken by the banks, final home loan approval remains subject to additional factors such as the property’s valuation and suitability as security for the loan amount, as well as any changes to the homebuyer’s financial circumstances between the time of issue and the formal home loan application,” explains Dyer.
